title: Respiration and Synthesis of Biological Molecules
description: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration, oxygen debt, and the synthesis of proteins, lipids and carbohydrates.
hero_image_caption: Germinating seeds consume stored glucose reserves through cellular respiration, driving the energy-intensive processes of early growth — a dramatic demonstration of respiration as a universal life force.
content_html:
What is Cellular Respiration?

Cellular respiration is a chemical process that occurs continuously in every living cell — animals, plants, fungi and bacteria all respire. It is not the same as breathing (ventilation) — respiration is a chemical reaction inside cells that transfers energy from glucose to a molecule called ATP. This energy drives all life processes, from muscle contraction and nerve impulse transmission to protein synthesis and active transport.

Respiration is an exothermic reaction — it transfers energy to the surroundings, which is why your body generates warmth. This transferred energy is vital: without it, cells could not carry out any of their functions.

Key Fact

Cellular respiration is a universal, exothermic chemical process that occurs continuously in all living cells. It transfers energy from glucose to ATP. It is NOT the same as breathing.

Aerobic Respiration

Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and occurs in the mitochondria. It produces a large yield of ATP, making it the most efficient form of respiration. This is why organisms with high energy demands (like mammals) rely primarily on aerobic respiration.

The word equation is:

$$\text{glucose} + \text{oxygen} \rightarrow \text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water} + \text{energy (ATP)}$$

The balanced symbol equation: \(C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O\)

Glucose is completely broken down in aerobic respiration. All the chemical energy stored in the glucose molecule is transferred — some to ATP for cellular work, and some as heat to the surroundings. This complete breakdown is why aerobic respiration releases much more ATP than anaerobic respiration.

Anaerobic Respiration

Anaerobic respiration occurs when oxygen is not available or in short supply — for example, during intense exercise when blood cannot deliver oxygen fast enough to muscles. It takes place in the cytoplasm and produces much less ATP than aerobic respiration because glucose is only partially broken down.

In animal cells: \(\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{lactic acid}\)

The incomplete breakdown of glucose produces lactic acid, which builds up in muscles during intense exercise, causing cramps and fatigue. After exercise, the body needs extra oxygen to break down the accumulated lactic acid — this is called the oxygen debt. You continue to breathe heavily after exercise to repay this debt: the extra oxygen is used to oxidise lactic acid in the liver, converting it back to glucose or carbon dioxide and water.

In plants and fungi (including yeast): \(\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{ethanol} + \text{carbon dioxide}\)

This process is called fermentation. It is used commercially in brewing (yeast produces ethanol for alcoholic drinks) and bread-making (yeast produces carbon dioxide that makes dough rise; the ethanol evaporates during baking).

The rate of respiration can be investigated using yeast in glucose solution or germinating peas. You can test for the products of respiration experimentally: breathing out through limewater turns it milky, confirming the presence of carbon dioxide. Using a temperature probe in a flask of germinating seeds or active yeast shows a temperature increase over time, confirming that respiration is exothermic.

For yeast fermentation, seal the flask with a bung connected to limewater via a delivery tube. As yeast respires anaerobically, carbon dioxide bubbles through the limewater, turning it milky. The rate at which this occurs can be compared across different sugar concentrations or temperatures.

Key Fact

Aerobic respiration (with oxygen, in mitochondria) produces a large yield of ATP. Anaerobic respiration (without oxygen, in cytoplasm) produces much less ATP. In animals it makes lactic acid; in fungi and plants it makes ethanol and carbon dioxide.

Synthesis of Biological Molecules

Respiration links to the synthesis and breakdown of key biological molecules. You need to understand the role of sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol as building blocks.

Carbohydrates: Simple sugars (monomers) such as glucose join together to form complex carbohydrates (polymers such as starch and glycogen). Glucose is the key monomer used in respiration. Starch is the storage form of glucose in plants; glycogen is the storage form in animals (stored in liver and muscles).

Proteins: Amino acid monomers join together in specific sequences (determined by DNA) to form protein polymers. Proteins are essential for enzymes, structural components (collagen, keratin), hormones (insulin) and antibodies. The sequence and type of amino acids determines the protein's shape and function.

Lipids: Formed from fatty acids and glycerol. Lipids are used for long-term energy storage (they contain more energy per gram than carbohydrates), thermal insulation, and making cell membranes. Lipids are not polymers in the strict sense because they are not made of repeating identical monomers.

The energy transferred by respiration is used both to build these molecules and to break them down. For example, energy from respiration drives the synthesis of proteins from amino acids, and the conversion of glucose to glycogen for storage. When the body needs energy, glycogen is broken back down into glucose for respiration.

Key Fact

Glucose monomers form starch (plant) or glycogen (animal) by polymerisation. Amino acids form proteins. Fatty acids and glycerol form lipids. Energy from respiration drives the synthesis of all these biological molecules.

Exercise and Respiration

During exercise, muscles need more energy, so the rate of respiration increases. The body responds by increasing heart rate (to deliver more oxygenated blood to muscles), increasing breathing rate and depth (to take in more oxygen and remove more carbon dioxide), and breaking down glycogen stored in muscles and the liver into glucose. If exercise is intense enough that blood cannot supply oxygen fast enough, muscles switch to anaerobic respiration, producing lactic acid. After exercise stops, continued heavy breathing supplies extra oxygen needed to break down lactic acid in the liver — this is the oxygen debt.
exam_tip_html: Never confuse respiration with breathing. For 3-mark 'explain' questions on exercise and respiration, link each adaptation to a reason: increased breathing rate → more oxygen delivered → aerobic respiration can continue. For extended responses on aerobic vs anaerobic, use the comparison table approach: location, oxygen requirement, products, ATP yield. In synthesis questions, always name the specific monomers (amino acids → proteins; glucose → starch/glycogen).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Cellular respiration is an exothermic process in all living cells that transfers energy from glucose to ATP. Aerobic respiration (mitochondria, with oxygen) produces a large ATP yield. Anaerobic respiration (cytoplasm, no oxygen) produces a small ATP yield — lactic acid in animals; ethanol + CO₂ in plants and fungi.
  • Oxygen debt is the extra oxygen needed after intense exercise to oxidise accumulated lactic acid in the liver.
  • Glucose monomers polymerise to form starch (plant storage) or glycogen (animal storage). Amino acids form proteins. Fatty acids and glycerol form lipids. Respiration provides the energy to build and break down these biological molecules.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a product of anaerobic respiration in yeast?
A) Water
B) Lactic acid
C) Ethanol
D) Glycogen
State where in the cell aerobic respiration takes place.
Describe two differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration in animal cells.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each for any two of the following:
• Aerobic respiration requires oxygen; anaerobic does not (1)
• Aerobic respiration takes place in mitochondria; anaerobic takes place in the cytoplasm (1)
• Aerobic respiration produces carbon dioxide and water; anaerobic produces lactic acid (1)
• Aerobic respiration produces a larger yield of ATP than anaerobic (1)
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by 'oxygen debt' and describe how the body repays it after intense exercise.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• During intense exercise, muscles switch to anaerobic respiration and lactic acid builds up (1)
• Oxygen debt is the extra oxygen required after exercise to break down / oxidise the accumulated lactic acid (1)
• The body repays the debt by continuing to breathe heavily after exercise, supplying oxygen to the liver where lactic acid is converted back to glucose or broken down to carbon dioxide and water (1)
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A student sets up an experiment to investigate the rate of fermentation in yeast at different temperatures. At 30°C, the yeast produces 40 cm³ of CO₂ in 5 minutes. At 40°C, it produces 70 cm³ in 5 minutes. Calculate the rate of CO₂ production at each temperature in cm³/min and explain which temperature shows a higher rate of anaerobic respiration.
practice_questions.marks:
Rate at 30°C = 40 ÷ 5 = 8 cm³/min (1)
Rate at 40°C = 70 ÷ 5 = 14 cm³/min (1)
40°C shows a higher rate (1)
Because at higher temperature, yeast enzymes have greater kinetic energy and collide more frequently with substrate, increasing the rate of enzyme-controlled reactions / approaching the optimum temperature (1)
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of respiration in the synthesis of biological molecules. Include reference to carbohydrates, proteins and lipids in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (up to 6 marks):
• Respiration transfers energy from glucose to ATP (1)
• This energy is used to drive the synthesis of biological molecules (1)
• Glucose monomers join together to form carbohydrate polymers: starch (storage in plants) and glycogen (storage in animals, liver and muscles) (1)
• Amino acids are joined in specific sequences (coded for by DNA) to form proteins; the sequence determines the protein's shape and function (1)
• Fatty acids and glycerol combine to form lipids, used for energy storage, cell membranes and thermal insulation (1)
• When energy is needed, these molecules can be broken back down — e.g. glycogen is hydrolysed to glucose which is then respired (1)

StudyVault Mastering: all three molecule classes covered with monomers named and roles linked to function.

knowledge_checks.q: Where does aerobic respiration take place in the cell?
Which equation correctly represents anaerobic respiration in animal cells?

options: The oxygen stored in haemoglobin during rest
The extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down accumulated lactic acid
The deficit of oxygen in the blood during aerobic respiration
The oxygen used by mitochondria during intense exercise
knowledge_checks.explanation: The correct answer is The extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down accumulated lactic acid.

knowledge_checks.explanation: Review the key terms and definitions covered in this lesson.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the word equation for aerobic respiration?
flashcard_questions.a: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy transferred to ATP)

flashcard_questions.q: What is the word equation for anaerobic respiration in animal cells?
flashcard_questions.a: Glucose → lactic acid (small amount of ATP released)

flashcard_questions.q: What is the word equation for fermentation in yeast?
Why is respiration described as exothermic?
flashcard_questions.a: Because it transfers energy to the surroundings, typically as heat — this is why organisms generate warmth during respiration.

flashcard_questions.q: What is oxygen debt and how is it repaid?
flashcard_questions.a: The extra oxygen needed after intense exercise to oxidise accumulated lactic acid. Repaid by continued heavy breathing, supplying oxygen to the liver to break down lactic acid.

flashcard_questions.q: What biological molecules are made from amino acids?
flashcard_questions.a: Proteins — amino acids are joined in a specific sequence (coded for by DNA) to form protein polymers with unique shapes and functions.
Fatty acids and glycerol — they are used for long-term energy storage, making cell membranes, and thermal insulation.

flashcard_questions.q: How can you test experimentally that respiration is exothermic?
flashcard_questions.a: Place a temperature probe in a flask of germinating seeds or active yeast — the temperature rises over time as respiration releases energy to the surroundings.

glossary_terms.definition: A universal chemical process occurring continuously in all living cells that breaks down glucose to transfer energy, supplying ATP for life processes.
Adenosine triphosphate — the molecule that stores and transfers energy within cells for biological processes.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, usually as heat, causing the temperature of the surroundings to increase.
A waste product of anaerobic respiration in animal cells that builds up in muscles during intense exercise, causing fatigue and cramps.
Anaerobic respiration in yeast and some plant cells that produces ethanol and carbon dioxide from glucose.
A small, single molecule that can bond with other monomers to form a polymer. Examples include simple sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol.
Organic acid molecules with a long hydrocarbon chain; combined with glycerol to form lipids such as fats and oils.
